Turf inside BVL's original screen-cage pools

Pool and lanai turf in Buenaventura Lakes runs $8–$18 per sq ft installed, typically $10–$16, as of September 2026, usually landing toward the upper half of that range. Most of the work is inside a screened cage original to a 1980s or 1990s home, where the concrete deck and the enclosure track shape the whole layout.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Turfing the deck strip inside a BVL pool cage

Say you have a 500 sq ft ring of concrete deck inside a 1994 screen enclosure, plus a 150 sq ft strip of real lawn just outside the cage wall. At the published residential range that's $5,200 to $11,700 installed for the combined 650 sq ft; since deck work runs the upper half of that range for the glue-down and drainage underlay, expect the deck portion closer to $14-$18 a foot and the outside strip closer to the standard $10-$16 band. The enclosure's footprint sets the deck cuts exactly; the outside strip has more flexibility, so any waste from an awkward cut is easier to absorb there than inside the fixed aluminum track.

Turf inside a 30- to 40-year-old screen enclosure

A pool cage built when Strafford Park or Coral Wood went up is now three to four decades old, and the concrete deck inside it rarely graded well even when new; sun and settling since then usually leave low spots that hold water after a rinse. Turf over that deck needs a drainage underlay between the concrete and the turf backing so water still has somewhere to go, plus edges glued rather than nailed, since driving a stake through a cage's existing slab isn't an option. Working inside the aluminum enclosure track also means every cut is measured to that fixed boundary rather than to an open yard where a little overage is easy to trim.

Why a shaded lanai floor tends to outlast an open deck border

Synthetic turf generally lasts ten to twenty years depending on UV stabilization, traffic, and infill, and a glued lanai floor under screen mesh in Buenaventura Lakes usually lands toward the higher end of that window, since the mesh cuts a meaningful amount of direct UV exposure compared with an open border baking in full sun all day. Foot traffic works the other direction: a well-used lanai floor near the door sees more steps over a season than a border strip along a fence line ever does. Which factor wins out depends on the household, but shade alone does not guarantee the longest possible lifespan.

Where the deck meets the yard outside the cage

Plenty of BVL pool lots have a narrow strip of real lawn between the screen enclosure and the property line, and that strip often backs a canal or a neighbor's fence rather than opening onto open grass. The transition from glued turf-on-concrete inside the cage to turf-on-base outside it needs a clean edge at the enclosure's foundation, and if that outside strip also sits within 10 feet of a canal, the water buffer applies there even though the cage itself is unaffected. Planning both sections as one job rather than two separate ones is what keeps that transition line straight instead of wandering along the screen track, and it also means the base under both areas gets graded to the same finished height from the start.

Why a lanai floor skips the rock base entirely

A screen enclosure or lanai floor around a Buenaventura Lakes pool is almost always bare concrete, so there is no soil underneath to build a normal base from. Instead of two to four inches of washed, open-graded crushed rock, the crew glues a thin drainage underlay straight to the slab, and that underlay carries splash and rinse water sideways toward whatever drain the deck already uses. An open border between the same cage and a side fence still gets the standard rock base, graded one to two percent, because that strip sits on native sand able to take water straight down. Two areas on one Buenaventura Lakes property, built on completely different foundations underneath the same green surface.

Does the pool itself count toward the ten-foot water setback?

A Buenaventura Lakes lot backing onto a retention pond, lake, or canal still has to keep turf at least ten feet from that water's edge unless a seawall or bulkhead already separates the two, and that rule reaches right up to the property line behind a pool cage even though the pool inside the cage does not count as a waterbody at all. Turf can run straight to the coping with no setback of its own. Confusing the two, and assuming a rear setback applies just because there is water somewhere on the property, can shrink a planned layout for no reason.

Building a border and a glued floor as one sequenced job

When a Buenaventura Lakes property gets both an open deck border and a glued lanai floor at the same visit, the rock base for the border goes in and compacts first, before the slab gets pressure washed for the glue-down section, so dust and loose fines from the soil work do not land on a clean, prepped slab. Compacting the border early also gives that section time to settle while the crew finishes prepping and gluing the floor, rather than rushing both areas to be ready on the same afternoon. The two areas finish on the same day even though they are built in a different order.

Keeping the deck drain clear inside a screen enclosure

A screen mesh keeps most large debris out of a Buenaventura Lakes lanai, but pollen, dust, and small leaves still settle on the turf and can work toward the deck drain over time, especially during the June-to-September rainy season when storms are frequent enough that the drain rarely gets a rest. A quick sweep or rinse toward the drain on a regular schedule keeps the whole underlay system doing what it was built for, since even a permeable backing cannot help much once the drain it feeds is the part that is actually clogged.

Heat and glare around a screened pool

A screen enclosure cuts direct sun less than most homeowners expect, so pool-deck turf in BVL still reaches the 120 to 150 degree range common on exposed Florida turf, and a low-E window on the house side of some of these lanais can add reflected heat on top of that. A hose rinse before anyone walks the deck barefoot drops the surface temperature fast, and checking which windows face the cage before finalizing turf placement avoids the melted spot that low-E glass can cause on a hot afternoon. The pool and lanai turf page covers drainage underlay options in more depth, and St. Cloud, another lake-heavy Osceola County town, sees the same screen-cage pattern on its older lots.

Questions people ask

Does pool-deck turf need a different base than a regular BVL lawn?

Yes, over existing concrete it needs a drainage underlay instead of washed crushed rock, since there's no soil underneath to grade or compact.

Will turf inside my screen enclosure still get hot?

It can. A screen cuts glare more than heat, so the same hose-rinse routine that cools open-yard turf works just as well on a lanai.

Can a window reflection actually melt turf on my BVL lanai?

Yes, if a low-E window or slider is aimed at it. This explainer covers the temperature threshold and how to spot the damage pattern before it spreads.
